Amazon River basin - Dense equatorial Forest - Low population density.
The Amazon basin is covered by thick equatorial forest with leached soil, heat, heavy rain and disease, so very few people live there.

Constrictive Pyramid - More old age Population - Low birth rate and least death rate.
A constrictive pyramid has a narrow base and a broad top, which is what a low birth rate together with a low death rate produces.

Industrial Region - Manufacturing Activities - Tata Iron and Steel Industries.
An industrial region is an area where manufacturing is concentrated, and the Tata iron and steel works at Jamshedpur is the example named.

Pampas Grassland - Commercial cattle rearing - South America.
The Pampas is the temperate grassland of South America, and commercial cattle rearing on large ranches is practised on it.

Private - Individual - Availability of Employment.
A private sector industry is owned by an individual or a company, and such industries are a major source of employment.

(C) development of iron-ore and coal mines.
The Appalachian region is mountainous, which by itself would keep people away. It is densely peopled because rich coal and iron ore are mined there, and mining, iron and steel and the towns that serve them have drawn population in.

(B) shallow seas, confluence of warm and cold ocean currents, growth of planktons, cold climate.
Shallow seas let sunlight reach the bed, the meeting of warm and cold currents brings up nutrients, planktons then multiply and feed the fish, and a cold climate helps preserve the catch.

(C) availability of rich deposits of coal and iron-ore.
The Appalachian coal field and the iron ore of the Great Lakes lie in and near this region, and iron and steel, on which the other industries were built, had to be located where both were available.

(B) The ganga-yamuna plain.
The northern plain of India is built by the Ganga, the Yamuna, the Indus and the Brahmaputra. The Nile, the Mississippi and the Amazon are in Africa, North America and South America.

(A) Natural resources.
Relief, soil, water, minerals and forests are physical. Sex ratio, school register ratio and employment are human and economic indicators, not physical factors.

(D) Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Hardwood trees are indeed found in the equatorial evergreen forest, and lumbering there is indeed not commercial. But the second is a CONSEQUENCE of the hardwood being heavy and the species scattered - it is a result of A, not an explanation of why hardwood grows there. So R does not explain A.

(D) Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Indian industry is concentrated in a few regions, and India is an agricultural country; both are true. But the concentration is caused by where coal, iron, ports, power and market are found together, not by the fact that most people farm. So R does not explain A.

(A) Only A is correct.
Tertiary activities take nothing directly from nature, so A is right. R is wrong, because tertiary activities include the exchange of goods - trade and commerce - as well as services, so they are not services alone.

(A) Only A is correct.
A formal region is uniform in the chosen feature and has distinct boundaries, so A is right. R is wrong, because it is the FUNCTIONAL region that is bounded by the reach of an economic activity; a formal region may be bounded by relief, climate, language or administration.

(C) Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
Physical and human factors do change over time, and the reason is exactly that the earth itself is dynamic and its physical and cultural environments keep varying. So R explains A.

(d) Prairie grassland region in North America.
The gold field of the Australian desert, the oil region of South West Asia and the Chota Nagpur plateau are all peopled because of minerals. The Prairie is densely settled because of wheat farming and cattle rearing, not because of mineral deposits.

(c) Motor industry.
Agriculture, hunting and lumbering all take a product directly from nature, so they are primary. The motor industry manufactures a vehicle out of processed material, so it is a secondary activity.

(a) Cement industries.
Clock making, diamond cutting and hairpin making use small quantities of light raw material and can be set up almost anywhere, so they are foot loose. Cement uses bulky limestone that loses weight in processing, so the plant must stand near the quarry.

(b) Fertile soil.
Antarctica has no permanent settlement because of very cold climate, frozen land and long winter. Fertile soil would be a reason FOR settlement, and in any case Antarctica has none, so it is the incorrect factor.

(d) Transport.
Atmospheric factors, relief and lakes are all parts of the natural environment and so belong to physical geography. Transport is built by people and is studied in human geography.

A literate person can take up skilled and better paid work, use new methods and know his rights, and literate parents look after health, nutrition and family size better. Literacy and the economic and social condition of a country therefore rise and fall together, which is why the literacy rate is used as an indicator of development.

India has extensive level plains with deep fertile alluvial soil, a monsoon climate with a long growing season, plentiful sunshine and a large supply of farm labour, and irrigation from rivers, canals, tanks and wells where rain is short. A very large population has also to be fed. So agriculture is practised on a large scale.

An industry needs raw material, power, water, capital, skilled labour, transport and a market together, and very few parts of the world have all of them. They are found together mainly in Western Europe, eastern North America, Japan and parts of Asia. Hence industries are concentrated in a few regions and their distribution is uneven.

Central Australia is a hot dry desert with almost no rainfall, no surface water, no fertile soil and very few people. There is no local labour force, no market and hardly any transport, and water and power for industry would have to be brought from far away. So industrial development is not found there.

An illiterate and poor population cannot take up skilled work, cannot use new technology and cannot save or invest, and it spends what it earns on bare necessities. The region's resources therefore remain unused, its productivity stays low and its people migrate away, so illiteracy and poverty hold back regional development.

Geography studies the natural environment and it studies human activity, and it treats the two as one subject because each acts on the other. This gives it a double character - it is a natural science and a social science at the same time, and it is divided into physical geography and human geography. That double character is what is meant by calling its nature dualistic.

Land use: how man USES a piece of land - for crops, pasture, forestry, housing, industry, transport or recreation. It is decided by people and changes quickly as needs change.
Land cover: what actually COVERS the surface of that land - forest, grass, crops, water, snow, sand, rock or built up area. It is a physical description, observed directly from the ground or from a satellite, and it changes more slowly. One land cover may carry several land uses, and a change of use often changes the cover.

Public sector industry: owned and run by the government, with capital from public funds; the aim is service to the country as much as profit; decisions are slow and bound by rules; examples are Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited.
Private sector industry: owned and run by an individual or a company, with private capital; the aim is profit; decisions are quick and management is flexible; examples are the Tata and Reliance industries.

Physical region: defined by a natural feature such as relief, climate, soil or vegetation, as in the Himalayan region or the Thar desert; its boundary is natural and changes only over a very long time.
Political region: defined by administration, as in a state, a district or a country; its boundary is drawn by people and can be changed by a decision, as when a new state is formed.

Regional development: the process by which a region's resources are used to raise the income, employment, literacy, health and standard of living of its people. It is a positive process and is the aim of planning.
Regional imbalance: the condition in which some regions have developed far more than others, so that income, industry and services are concentrated in a few while the rest stay backward. It is the problem that regional development is meant to remove.

Possibilism: the view that nature offers a range of possibilities and that man chooses among them according to his culture and technology. Vidal de la Blache was its chief supporter, and irrigated deserts, reclaimed land in the Netherlands and settlement in the Arctic are cited as proof.
Determinism: the view that the physical environment decides human activity, and that man can do only what nature permits. Ratzel and Semple were its supporters, and they held that climate and relief shape a people's occupations, character and history.

Birth rate and death rate together decide natural growth.
When both are high, growth is very slow, because the many births are cancelled by the many deaths.
When the death rate falls while the birth rate stays high, the gap between the two widens and the population grows very fast. This is the stage of population explosion.
When the birth rate also begins to fall, the gap narrows again and growth slows.
When both are low, growth is nearly nil and the population becomes stable, and if the birth rate falls below the death rate the population declines.
So it is not either rate by itself but the GAP between them that decides how fast a population grows.

Mixed land use means that a single area of a town is put to more than one use at the same time - shops on the ground floor, offices above them and dwellings above those, with workshops and godowns in the same lane.
It is found chiefly in the old core of a city, where land is scarce and dear and where the town grew before planning.
Its advantages are that work, shopping and home lie close together, so travel is short, the street is alive through the day and land is used to the full.
Its disadvantages are congestion, noise, traffic, shortage of parking and open space, and the risk of fire and pollution where small industry stands among houses.
Modern town planning therefore allows mixed use deliberately in some zones and separates the uses in others.

Hunting is the killing of wild animals for meat, skin, horn, ivory or sport, and gathering is the collecting of wild fruit, roots and honey.
As a subsistence occupation it does little harm, because the tribes that practise it take only what they need and move on.
Commercial and indiscriminate hunting is a different matter. It has driven many species to the edge of extinction - the tiger, rhinoceros, elephant, whale and many birds - for ivory, fur, skin and horn.
Every species is a link in a food chain, so removing one upsets the whole chain: the prey of a lost predator multiplies and destroys vegetation, and the animals that depended on that vegetation then die out.
The loss of a species also ends the pollination, seed dispersal and scavenging it performed, so forests and grasslands themselves degrade.
Hence hunting is now restricted by law, and national parks, sanctuaries and biosphere reserves have been created to protect the ecosystem.

No industry can work without transport.
It brings the raw material, fuel and machinery to the factory, and carries the finished goods to the market.
Cheap transport lowers the delivered cost of the product and widens the area over which it can be sold, so it decides how large a market the industry can serve.
The kind of transport available influences WHERE the industry is located: a bulky raw material goes by rail or water, so industries using it stand near a railhead or a port, as the iron and steel industry does.
Fast transport makes industry in perishable goods - milk, fruit, fish and flowers - possible at all.
Transport also carries the workers to the factory, and it links one industry to another, since the product of one is the raw material of the next.
So a region with good roads, railways, ports and airports attracts industry, and a region without them does not.

An artificial satellite is a man-made body put into orbit round the earth, and a communication satellite receives a signal from one point and sends it on to another.
Its importance: it carries telephone, television, radio and internet signals across oceans and over mountains without any cable; it gives instant contact between any two places on earth; it carries weather pictures and cyclone warnings that save life; it makes tele-education and telemedicine possible in remote villages; it supports GPS and navigation; it is used in survey, mapping and resource exploration through remote sensing; and it is essential in disaster management and defence.
INSAT and GSAT in India are examples.
Between 30 degrees N and 60 degrees N, and between 30 degrees S and 55 degrees S.

Human factors are those created by people themselves. They can gather population into a place the physical setting would not favour, and empty a place that it does.
Economic activity is the strongest of them. Wherever industry, mining, trade or plantation work offers wages, people gather. The Ruhr in Germany, the Damodar valley in India and Kimberley in South Africa are crowded because of coal, iron and diamonds, not because of their relief or climate.
Transport and communication decide whether a place can be reached and its produce sold. Population is dense along river valleys, coasts, railway lines and highways, and thin where there are no routes, as in the interior of the Amazon basin.
Urbanisation draws people continuously from village to town, because the town concentrates work, education, medical care and entertainment. Mumbai, Delhi, Tokyo and New York have grown in this way.
Political factors matter greatly. Peace, law and order and a settled government attract people and investment, while war and persecution empty a region, as in Syria. Government policy can create population where there was none, as Brazil did by building Brasilia and India by building Chandigarh.
Social and cultural factors work the same way. Religious centres such as Varanasi and Mecca hold large populations, and so do educational centres such as Pune and Oxford.
Technology allows people to live where they could not before, by irrigating deserts as in Israel and Rajasthan, by air conditioning, and by reclaiming land from the sea as in the Netherlands.
So the physical setting decides where people CAN live, and the human factors decide where they actually DO live.

Trade is the exchange of goods and services, and whether it takes place at all, and in what direction, is decided by several factors.
Geographical diversity is the first and the most important. No region has everything it needs, because relief, climate, soil and minerals differ from place to place. A region sells what it has in surplus and buys what it lacks, so the difference between regions is what creates trade.
Natural resources decide what a country has to offer. West Asia exports oil, Australia wool and minerals, Brazil coffee and Sri Lanka tea, because those are what their land yields.
Specialisation and the level of technology decide what a country can make. A developed country exports machinery, vehicles and chemicals and imports raw material, while a developing country does the reverse.
Transport makes the exchange physically possible, and cheap transport decides how far goods can be sent. Sea routes, canals such as the Suez and the Panama, container ships and air cargo have each enlarged world trade by cutting distance, time or loss.
Population and the market decide how much can be sold. A large population with purchasing power, as in the U.S.A., China and India, attracts goods from everywhere; a small or poor population does not.
Government policy can encourage or throttle trade through tariffs, quotas, subsidies, trade agreements and currency rules. Membership of groups such as the WTO, the European Union and SAARC widens trade among members.
Political relations matter, since war, sanctions or hostility can stop trade between two countries however well placed they are, while friendly relations increase it.
Banking, insurance, warehousing and communication support trade at every step, by financing the goods, covering the risk, storing them and carrying the information.
Finally the level of development itself is decisive, because a developed economy produces a larger surplus and can buy more, and so takes the larger share of world trade.
